In [[statistical hypothesis testing]], the error exponent of a hypothesis testing procedure is the rate at which the probabilities of Type I and Type II decay exponentially with the size of the sample used in the test. For example, if the probability of error <math>P_{\mathrm{error}}</math> of a test decays as <math>e^{-n \beta}</math>, where <math>n</math> is the sample size, the error exponent is <math>\beta</math>.

Formally, the error exponent of a test is defined as the limiting value of the ratio of the negative [[logarithm]] of the error probability to the sample size for large sample sizes:  <math>\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{-\log P_\text{error}}{n}</math>. Error exponents for different hypothesis tests are computed using [[Sanov's theorem]] and other results from [[large deviations theory]]. There are various methods used to show that an error exponent is achievable, including the [[Likelihood-ratio test|likelihood ratio]] ([[Neyman–Pearson lemma|which is known to be optimal in certain circumstances]]), and the [[Empirical measure|empirical distribution]].<ref Name="HoeffdingMultinomial">{{Cite journal |last=Hoeffding |first=Wassily |year=1965 |title=Asymptotically Optimal Tests for Multinomial Distributions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2238145 |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=369–401 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177700150 |jstor=2238145 |issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free }}</ref> Error exponents are sometimes referred to as error rates, due to the connection between hypothesis testing and [[information theory]].<ref name="HypTestingAndInfoTheory"/>

==Error exponents in binary hypothesis testing==
Consider a binary hypothesis testing problem in which observations are modeled as [[independent and identically distributed random variables]] under each hypothesis. Let <math> Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n </math> denote the observations. Let <math> f_0 </math> denote the [[probability density function]] of each observation <math>Y_i</math> under the null hypothesis <math>H_0</math> and let <math> f_1 </math> denote the probability density function of each observation <math>Y_i</math> under the alternate hypothesis <math>H_1</math>.

In this case there are [[Type I and type II errors|two possible error events]]. Error of type I, also called [[False positives and false negatives#False positive error|false positive]], occurs when the null hypothesis is true and it is wrongly rejected. Error of type II, also called [[False positives and false negatives#False negative error|false negative]], occurs when the alternate hypothesis is true and null hypothesis is not rejected. The probability of type I error is denoted <math>P (\mathrm{error}\mid H_0)</math> and the probability of type II error is denoted <math>P (\mathrm{error}\mid H_1)</math>. In some fields, the type I error is denoted by <math>\alpha_n</math> and the type II error is denoted by <math>\beta_n</math>.

===Optimal error exponent for Neyman–Pearson testing===
In the Neyman–Pearson<ref name="NeymanPearson1933">{{citation | last1 = Neyman | first1 = J. | authorlink1 = Jerzy Neyman| last2 = Pearson | first2 = E. S. | authorlink2 = Egon Pearson| doi = 10.1098/rsta.1933.0009 | title = On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses | journal = [[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A]] | volume = 231 | issue = 694–706 | pages = 289–337 | year = 1933 | jstor = 91247 |bibcode = 1933RSPTA.231..289N | url = http://www.stats.org.uk/statistical-inference/NeymanPearson1933.pdf | doi-access = free }}</ref> version of binary hypothesis testing, one is interested in minimizing the probability of type II error <math>P (\text{error}\mid H_1)</math> subject to the constraint that the probability of type I error <math>P (\text{error}\mid H_0)</math> is less than or equal to a pre-specified level <math>\alpha</math>. In this setting, the optimal testing procedure is a [[likelihood-ratio test]].<ref name=LR>{{cite book|title=Testing Statistical Hypotheses|edition=3|isbn=978-0-387-98864-1|last1=Lehmann|first1=E. L.|authorlink1 = Erich Leo Lehmann|first2=Joseph P.|last2=Romano|year=2005|publisher=Springer|location=New York}}</ref> Furthermore, the optimal test guarantees that the type II error probability decays exponentially in the sample size <math>n</math> according to <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{- \log P (\mathrm{error}\mid H_1)}{n} = D(f_0\parallel f_1)</math>.<ref name=CT>{{cite book|title=Elements of Information Theory|edition=2|last1=Cover|first1=Thomas M.|authorlink1=Thomas M. Cover|first2=Joy A.|last2=Thomas|year=2006|publisher=Wiley-Interscience|location=New York}}</ref> The error exponent <math>D(f_0\parallel f_1)</math> is the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] between the probability distributions of the observations under the two hypotheses. This exponent is also referred to as the Chernoff–Stein lemma exponent.

===Optimal error exponent for average error probability in Bayesian hypothesis testing===
In the [[Bayesian]] version of binary hypothesis testing one is interested in minimizing the average error probability under both hypothesis, assuming a [[prior probability]] of occurrence on each hypothesis. Let <math> \pi_0 </math> denote the prior probability of hypothesis <math> H_0 </math>. In this case the average error probability is given by <math> P_\text{ave} = \pi_0 P (\text{error}\mid H_0) + (1-\pi_0)P (\text{error}\mid H_1)</math>. In this setting again a likelihood ratio test is optimal and the optimal error decays as <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{- \log P_\text{ave} }{n} = C(f_0,f_1)</math> where <math>C(f_0,f_1)</math> represents the Chernoff-information between the two distributions defined as <math> C(f_0,f_1) = \max_{\lambda \in [0,1]} \left[-\log \int (f_0(x))^\lambda (f_1(x))^{(1-\lambda)} \, dx \right]</math>.<ref name="CT" />

=== Trade-off between type I and II error ===
A more explicit tradeoff between the type I and type II error is observed when the type I error is constrained to decay exponentially, and the type II error is minimized. If we require <math> P(\text{error} | H_0) < e^{-n r } </math> for some <math> r < D(f_1\| f_0)</math>, then the optimal type II error exponent is described by <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} -\frac{1}{n} \log P(\text{error} | H_1) = H_r(f_0\parallel f_1) </math>. Here  <math>H(f_0\parallel f_1)</math> is the [[Hoeffding divergence]]<ref>{{Citation |last1=Ogawa |first1=Tomohiro |title=On Error Exponents in Quantum Hypothesis Testing |year=2002 |arxiv=quant-ph/0206151 |last2=Hayashi |first2=Masahito |bibcode=2002quant.ph..6151O }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Hoeffding |first=Wassily |chapter=On Probabilities of Large Deviations |year=1994 |title=The Collected Works of Wassily Hoeffding |pages=473–490 |editor-last=Fisher |editor-first=N. I. |series=Springer Series in Statistics |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-0865-5_29 |access-date=2026-03-02 |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0865-5_29 |isbn=978-1-4612-0865-5 |editor2-last=Sen |editor2-first=P. K.}}</ref><ref name="HypTestingAndInfoTheory">{{Cite journal |last=Blahut |first=R. |year=1974 |title=Hypothesis testing and information theory |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=405–417 |doi=10.1109/TIT.1974.1055254 |bibcode=1974ITIT...20..405B |issn=1557-9654}}</ref> described by {{Equation|1= H_r(f_0 \parallel f_1) = \max_{0\leq s \leq 1} \frac{\Psi(s) - (1-s)r}{s} |2=1}}where <math>\Psi(s) = - \log \int dx\  f_0(x)^{1-s} f_1(x)^s</math>.

=== Second Order Analysis ===
Sometimes, the above considerations are described as the first order error exponents of hypothesis testing, meaning the analysis of 
{{ Equation | \lim_{n \to \infty}-\frac{1}{n}\log \mathbb{P}_{H_1}[\text{error}] }}
However, it is also possible to analyze higher order error exponents, for example the second order error exponent. If the first order error exponent is given by <math>I_1</math>, then the second order error exponent is taken to be
{{Equation| -\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{ \sqrt{n} } \left( -\log \left( \mathbb{P}_{H_1}[\text{error}]\right) - nI_1\right) }}

Second order analysis of hypothesis testing has been studied for several types of problems: simple hypothesis testing,<ref name="SecondOrderSimple">{{cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Lin |last2=Tan |first2=Vincent Y F |last3=Motani |first3=Mehul |title=Second-order asymptotically optimal statistical classification |journal=Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA |date=22 January 2019 |volume=9 |issue=1 |doi=10.1093/imaiai/iay023 |url=https://academic.oup.com/imaiai/article-abstract/9/1/81/5292489 |language=en |issn=2049-8764 | arxiv=1806.00739}}</ref> [[Universal hypothesis testing|One sample universal hypothesis testing]],<ref name="UniversalOneSample">{{cite book |last1=Harsha |first1=K. V. |last2=Ravi |first2=Jithin |last3=Koch |first3=Tobias |chapter=Second-Order Asymptotics of Hoeffding-Like Hypothesis Tests |title=2022 IEEE Information Theory Workshop (ITW) |date=November 2022 |pages=654–659 |doi=10.1109/ITW54588.2022.9965931 |arxiv=2205.05631 |bibcode=2022itw..conf...35H |hdl=10016/36612 |isbn=978-1-6654-8341-4 }}</ref> and two-sample universal problems.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Harsha |first1=K. V. |title=Second-Order Asymptotics of Two-Sample Tests |date=2026-01-14 |last2=Ravi |first2=Jithin |last3=Koch |first3=Tobias | arxiv=2601.09196}}</ref> The second order error exponent is sometimes called the relative entropy variance.<ref name="SecondOrderSimple" />
